title: Following along with Sold a Story 2
author: John Wills Lloyd
summary: John Wills Lloyd, who studied under Siegfried Engelmann, Douglas Carnine, and Wesley Becker in the 1970s, listens to American Public Media's Sold a Story 2 podcast on Direct Instruction and shares graphs he used in courses about Project Follow Through. He explains how districts picked sponsor models at a show-and-tell meeting and received the same health, nutrition, and staffing benefits whichever model they chose. Using Abt Associates data, he shows bar graphs comparing nine models on basic skills, cognitive, and affective outcomes, plus the share of children a year or more behind grade level. The Direct Instruction model leads on basic skills and holds up on higher order and self-concept measures, and it left fewer students far behind. Lloyd argues the design of the study blunts common objections, such as a single good teacher or a lucky test, and notes critiques like House et al. (1978) will be addressed later. He also stresses that Follow Through was not a special education study.
points: Follow Through let districts choose among sponsor models while holding non-instructional services roughly constant, so differences in outcomes point at instruction.
The Direct Instruction model outperformed the comparison models on basic skills, and also did well on cognitive and affective measures that critics expected it to lag.
Models with fewer students more than a year below grade level performed better, which Lloyd links to current interest in strong Tier 1 core instruction.
Multiple independent tests and many classrooms across years make it hard to explain the results away as one good teacher or the wrong test.
Lloyd reminds readers the study was not limited to students with disabilities and promises a later treatment of criticisms such as House et al. (1978).
quotes: The structure and conduct of the FT study rules out a lot of potential objections to the results. Detractors cannot get away with saying, “Oh, it was just one good teacher; that’s why those kids did well.
It is pretty obvious that in the areas of word reading, spelling, computing, and language (as measured by the Metropolitan Achievement Test), the DI model beat the pants off all the others.
The LEAs literally attended a meeting where representatives of each of the sponsors did a show-and-tell about what they would hope to accomplish in classrooms affiliated with their model.
As we shall see, the different counting rules do not make much of a difference. The pattern of results is consistent regardless of which counting system one used.
This should be a big hint to those folks who today are interested in “Tier 1” core instruction, especially because these results come from classrooms and schools that faced terrific challenges
I also want to remind readers that this was not a special education study. The participating students were not selected because they had disabilities.
It is hard to say, “Well, they just got the right test,” when there were multiple different tests administered by independent testers.
